candidate.answerReason: The common whole-cent price must be 1 or 13 cents. The 30-student limit rules out 1 cent, leaving 15 sixth-grade buyers and 11 seventh-grade buyers, a difference of 4.

methods.label: Use common factors and the student limit
methods.explanation:
Work in cents, so the two groups spent \(143\) cents and \(195\) cents. Because each buyer bought one pencil at the same positive whole-cent price, that price must divide both totals.

The factor pairs of \(143\) are \(1\times143\) and \(11\times13\), so its positive factors are \(1,11,13,143\). Among these, only \(1\) and \(13\) also divide \(195\). A price of \(1\) cent would require \(195\) sixth graders to buy pencils, but there are only \(30\) sixth graders. Thus each pencil costs \(13\) cents.

The numbers of buyers are therefore
\[
195\div13=15\quad\text{sixth graders},
\]
\[
143\div13=11\quad\text{seventh graders}.
\]
The sixth-grade count is within the limit of \(30\), and the difference is \(15-11=\boxed{4}\), choice D.
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary factor lists, total-price relationships, and division. The student limit selects the valid common factor.

review.mathematicalCheck: The positive whole-cent price must divide both 143 and 195. Their common factors are exactly 1 and 13. The one-cent price would require 195 sixth-grade buyers, exceeding 30; thirteen cents gives feasible counts 15 and 11, whose difference is 4. The argument establishes uniqueness.
